---
title: "Internal Migration in Canada"
subtitle: "Push and Pull Factors, Lag Effects, and Covid-19 Structural Shift"
---

## Overview

Regulations and stories about immigration have pervaded Canadian news in recent years. Much less attention is being paid to internal migration. Yet the study of internal migration can inform planning for infrastructure and public services, as well as helping researchers understand the change in the population composition of different regions. While the Canadian population is still concentrated in a few areas such as Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, these CMAs have seen an exodus in recent years owing to high housing cost and general cost of living (McQuillan, 2024). A push factor is a local condition that encourages residents to leave, e.g., high rent, elevated unemployment, or an ageing population. A pull factor is a condition that attracts residents, e.g., employment opportunity, affordability.

This project studies CMA-level net internal migration rates from 2001 to 2024 under two distinct research goals.

[Primary — Prediction (RQ1, RQ2)]{.lead-label} How much variance in net interprovincial and intraprovincial migration rates can be predicted by push–pull structural factors, and which model family generalises best out of time?

[Secondary — Inference (RQ3)]{.lead-label} Is the 2020–2024 COVID period associated with a structural shift in migration, and does that shift differ by CMA size?

## Findings

**Prediction.** Push and pull factors explain more variance in CMA-level intraprovincial migration rate (Random Forest holdout R² = 0.42) than interprovincial rate (Random Forest holdout R² = 0.30). The best models are tree-based, beating linear baselines by approximately 0.20 in holdout R² for both outcomes. The dominant predictors differ by outcome: `rd_provincial` and `share_65plus` rank highest for interprovincial rates, while `intl_inmigration` and `log_population` lead for intraprovincial rates. Interprovincial flows are labour and opportunity driven, while intraprovincial flows are housing and demographic driven.

**Inference.** On the interprovincial side, a significant post-2020 structural shift is detected for large CMAs (coefficient −0.72, p = 0.04). On the intraprovincial side the linear interaction is not statistically significant (p = 0.14), but the GAM partial dependency plot shows a clear non-linear 2020–2022 spike. Baseline intraprovincial gains for medium (+2.60) and small (+2.83) CMAs over large CMAs are robust and large relative to any estimated COVID shift, suggesting the suburban growth pattern overshadows the pandemic shock.

## Data

Five Statistics Canada tables, all accessed via the public bulk CSV endpoint (no API key required):

| Table | Content | Geography |
|---|---|---|
| 17-10-0149-01 | Components of population change (net migration outcomes) | CMA |
| 17-10-0148-01 | Population estimates (age structure) | CMA |
| 34-10-0133-01 | CMHC average rents | CMA |
| 14-10-0020-01 | Unemployment and participation rate | Province |
| 27-10-0273-02 | R&D expenditures by performing sector | Province |

After cleaning and merging, the panel contains 40 CMAs × 24 years = **960 CMA-year observations**.
